'''George Beals Schaller''' (born May 26, 1933<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eliteprospects.com/player/1001047/george-schaller|title=George Schaller at eliteprospects.com|website=www.eliteprospects.com}}</ref>) is an American [[mammalogist]], [[natural history|biologist]], [[conservation movement|conservationist]] and author. Schaller is recognized by many as the world's preeminent field [[biologist]], studying wildlife throughout Africa, Asia and South America.<ref name="msu" /><ref name="time">{{cite magazine|url=http://www.time.com/time/specials/2007/article/0,28804,1663317_1663323_1669908,00.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071021013325/http://www.time.com/time/specials/2007/article/0,28804,1663317_1663323_1669908,00.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 21, 2007|title=George Schaller – Heroes of the Environment|access-date=October 19, 2007|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|author=Bryan Walsh | date=October 17, 2007}}</ref><ref name="man">{{Cite news|url=http://www.hindu.com/mag/2006/10/01/stories/2006100100120500.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061017222513/http://www.hindu.com/mag/2006/10/01/stories/2006100100120500.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 17, 2006|title= Man of Nature: A freewheeling chat with environmentalist George Schaller.|access-date=October 5, 2007|work=[[The Hindu]]|author=K. Pradeep|location=Chennai, India|date=October 1, 2006}}</ref><ref name="uofa">{{Cite web|url=http://www.gi.alaska.edu/ScienceForum/ASF18/1813.html|title=Biologist sees value in unchanged landscape|access-date=October 19, 2007|publisher=Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska – Fairbanks|year=2006|author=Ned Rozell|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120503184821/http://www2.gi.alaska.edu/ScienceForum/ASF18/1813.html|archive-date=May 3, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> Born in Berlin, Schaller grew up in Germany, but moved to [[Missouri]] as a teen. He is vice president of [[Panthera Corporation]] and serves as chairman of their Cat Advisory Council. Schaller is also a senior conservationist at the [[Bronx Zoo]]-based [[Wildlife Conservation Society]].<ref name="lang">{{Cite web|url=http://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/best-of-adventure-2007/wildlife/george-schaller.html|title=Lifetime Achievement: Biologist George Schaller|access-date=October 5, 2007|work=[[National Geographic]]|year=2007|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071014014343/http://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/best-of-adventure-2007/wildlife/george-schaller.html|archive-date=October 14, 2007}}</ref><ref name="hindutwo">{{Cite news|url=http://www.hindu.com/nic/landuseplan.htm|title= A country like India must have a land use plan|access-date=October 20, 2007|work=[[The Hindu]]|year=2006|author=G. Ananthakrishnan|location=Chennai, India}}</ref>

==Early life==

Schaller was born in Berlin, Germany. He received his [[Bachelor of Science|Bachelor of Biological Science]] degree from the [[University of Alaska]] in 1955, and went on to the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] to obtain his [[PhD]] in 1962.<ref name="cas" /><ref name="interview">{{Cite web|url=http://www.sanctuaryasia.com/interviews/gbschaller.php|title=Dr. George Schaller Interview|access-date=October 19, 2007|publisher=Sanctuary Asia|year=2006|author=Sanctuary Asia|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071008151005/http://www.sanctuaryasia.com/interviews/gbschaller.php|archive-date=October 8, 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref> From 1962 to 1963, he was a fellow at the Behavioral Sciences department of [[Stanford University]]. From 1963 to 1966, Schaller served as research associate for the [[Johns Hopkins University]] [[Pathology|pathobiology]] department, and from 1966 to 1972, served as the [[Rockefeller University]]'s and [[New York Zoological Society]]'s research associate in research and animal behavior as part of the Institute for Research in Animal Behavior.<ref name="icp">{{Cite web|url=http://www.expo-cosmos.or.jp/jusyou/1996_e.html|title=The Prizewinner, 1996: George Beals Schaller|access-date=October 5, 2007|publisher=International Cosmos Prize|year=1996|author=International Cosmos Prize|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071005080723/http://www.expo-cosmos.or.jp/jusyou/1996_e.html|archive-date=October 5, 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref> From 1972 to 1979, he served as coordinator of the Center for Field Biology and Conservation, which replaced the IRAB. He then served as director of the [[New York Zoological Society]]'s International Conservation Program from 1979 to 1988.<ref name="natgeo2">{{Cite web|url=http://www7.nationalgeographic.com/ngm/0610/voices.html?fs=www3.nationalgeographic.com&fs=plasma.nationalgeographic.com|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130129134416/http://www7.nationalgeographic.com/ngm/0610/voices.html?fs=www3.nationalgeographic.com&fs=plasma.nationalgeographic.com|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 29, 2013|title=Voices: George Schaller|access-date=October 5, 2007|work=National Geographic|year=2006}}</ref>

==Mountain gorilla research==

In 1959, when Schaller was 26, he traveled to Central Africa to study and live with the [[mountain gorilla]]s (''Gorilla beringei beringei'') of the [[Virunga Volcanoes]].<ref name="time" /><ref name="Natgeo">{{Cite web|url=http://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/best-of-adventure-2007/wildlife/george-schaller-leopards-lions-pandas.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080307032528/http://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/best-of-adventure-2007/wildlife/george-schaller-leopards-lions-pandas.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 7, 2008|title=Biologist George Schaller's 50-Year Battle|access-date=October 5, 2007|work=National Geographic|year=2007|author=Ryan Bradley}}</ref><ref name="cic">{{Cite web |url=http://school.discoveryeducation.com/ontv/championsofthewild_1006.html |title=Mountain Gorillas |access-date=October 5, 2007 |publisher=[[Animal Planet]] |year=2006 |author=Cable in the Classroom |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080507072314/http://school.discoveryeducation.com/ontv/championsofthewild_1006.html |archive-date=May 7, 2008|author-link=Cable in the Classroom }}</ref> Little was known about the life of gorillas in the wild until the publication of ''The Mountain Gorilla: Ecology and Behavior'' in 1963, that first conveyed to the general public just how profoundly intelligent and gentle gorillas really are, contrary to then-common beliefs. Schaller also, in 1964, recounted this epic two-year study in ''The Year of the Gorilla'', which also provides a broader historical perspective on the efforts to save one of humankind's nearest relatives from the brink of extinction.<ref name="Natgeo" />

The American zoologist [[Dian Fossey]], with assistance from the [[National Geographic Society]] and [[Louis Leakey]], followed Schaller's ground-breaking field research on mountain gorillas in the Virungas.<ref name="lang" /> Schaller and Fossey were instrumental in dispelling the public perception of gorillas as brutes, by demonstrably establishing the deep compassion and social intelligence evident among gorillas, and how very closely their behavior parallels that of humans.<ref name="interview" />

{{blockquote|No one who looks into a gorilla's eyes – intelligent, gentle, vulnerable – can remain unchanged, for the gap between ape and human vanishes; we know that the gorilla still lives within us.  Do gorillas also recognize this ancient connection?<ref name="quote">{{cite journal | last =Schaller | first =George B. | title =Gentle Gorillas, Turbulent Times | journal=National Geographic | volume = 188 | issue = 4 | pages = 66 | date =October 1995 }}</ref>}}

==Conservation career==
In 1963-1964, Schaller and his wife were in Kanha National Park, India where they studied tigers. In 1966, Schaller and his wife traveled to [[Tanzania]] to live in the [[Serengeti]], and Schaller conducted one of the first studies of social behavior and movement of Africa's big cats.<ref name="uofa" /><ref name="Natgeo" /> Schaller appeared as himself on the December 6, 1965 episode of the [[CBS]] gameshow ''[[To Tell the Truth]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=To Tell the Truth |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OESiPX6qYBU |website=[[YouTube]] | date=August 3, 2017 |access-date=13 May 2024}}</ref>

In his 1972 work ''The Tree Where Man Was Born'', author [[Peter Matthiessen]] described Schaller as "single-minded, not easy to know". Matthiessen went on to say Schaller was "a stern pragmatist" who "takes a hard-eyed look at almost everything", "lean and intent", and in 1978's ''The Snow Leopard'' Matthiessen wrote that by that time, some considered Schaller the world's finest field biologist.<ref name="msu" /><ref name="man" /><ref name="matt">{{cite book |author=Matthiessen, Peter |title=The Snow Leopard (Penguin Nature Classics) |publisher=Penguin Books |location=New York |year=1978 |isbn=0-14-025508-7 |page=[https://archive.org/details/snowleopard00matt_0/page/352 352 pages] |url=https://archive.org/details/snowleopard00matt_0/page/352 }}</ref>

In the fall of 1973, Schaller went to the remote [[Himalayas|Himalayan]] region of [[Dolpo]], an area of [[Nepal]] occupied by people of the [[Tibet]]an culture and ethnicity.<ref name="interview" /> Schaller was there to study the Himalayan [[Bharal]], (blue sheep), and possibly glimpse the elusive [[snow leopard]], an animal rarely spotted in the wild. Schaller is one of only two Westerners known to have seen a snow leopard in Nepal between 1950 and 1978. Accompanying him on the trip was Matthiessen, and as a result of the trip, Matthiessen wrote ''The Snow Leopard'', (1978) detailing the accounts of their travels and research, which won two U.S. [[National Book Awards]].<ref name="winners">1979 Contemporary Thought and 1980 General Nonfiction (paperback). There were more than 30 awards for paperback books, 1980 to 1983 only, and ''The Snow Leopard'' was the only double winner. <!-- source is manual count and inspection --><br/>[http://www.nationalbook.org/nbawinners_category.html "National Book Award Winners: 1950–2009"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090731113541/http://www.nationalbook.org/nbawinners_category.html |date=July 31, 2009 }}. National Book Foundation: Awards. Retrieved January 5, 2012.</ref> Schaller is referred to throughout the book as "GS".<ref name="matt" /><ref name="matthiessen">{{cite book |author=Matthiessen, Peter |title=The Snow Leopard |publisher=Viking Press |location=New York |year=1978 |isbn=0-670-65374-8 |page=338 pages}}</ref>

In the late 1970s, Schaller spent time in Brazil studying the [[jaguar]], [[capybara]], "alligator" ([[caiman]]), and other animals of the region.<ref name="icp" />

In 1980, as part of a cooperative project between the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) and China, Schaller carried out field research on the [[giant panda]] in the Wolong Nature Reserve in Sichuan Province. He was the first Westerner to do so since before the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, and he co-authored the resulting monograph, [https://archive.org/details/giantpandasofwol0000unse The Giant Pandas of Wolong]. Schaller sought to refute the notion that the panda population was declining due to natural [[bamboo]] die-offs.<ref name="interview" /><ref name="icp" /> Instead, Schaller found the panda's popularity was leading to its frequent capture, and was the biggest threat to the population. Schaller also found evidence that pandas were originally [[carnivore]]s, but underwent an evolutionary change to accommodate a diet of [[bamboo]], which is difficult to digest, reducing competition with other animals for food.<ref name="icp" />  Since Schaller's research, the panda population has increased in the wild by 45 percent.<ref name="Natgeo" /> During his time in China, Schaller would hand out cards to wildlife hunters that read: "All beings tremble at punishment, to all, life is dear. Comparing others to oneself, one should neither kill nor cause to kill."<ref name="Natgeo" /> Schaller has spent more time in China than he has spent at his home in Connecticut.<ref name="lang" /> In 1993, Schaller wrote [https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/L/bo3631069.html The Last Panda], a meditation not only on the fate of the species but on the politics of conservation more broadly.

In 1988, Schaller and his wife traveled to China's [[Tibetan Plateau|Chang Tang]] (Qiang Tang) region to study the [https://china.wcs.org/Wildlife/Tibetan-Antelope.aspx Tibetan antelope], or ''chiru'', and became one of the first westerners permitted to enter the remote region.<ref name="book">{{cite book |author=Schaller, George B. |title=Tibet's Hidden Wilderness: Wildlife and Nomads of the Chang Tang Reserve |publisher=Harry N. Abrams |location=New York |year=1997 |isbn=0-8109-3893-6 |page=168 pages}}</ref>

In 1994, Schaller and Dr. [[Alan Rabinowitz]] were the first scientists to uncover the rare [[saola]], a [[forest]]-dwelling [[bovine]] in [[Laos]]. Later that year, Schaller rediscovered the Vietnamese [[Indo-chinese warty pig|warty pig]], once thought extinct. In 1996, he located a herd of [[Tibetan red deer]], also thought extinct.<ref name="lang" /><ref name="Natgeo" />

In 2003, Schaller returned to Chang Tang, and found the wildlife in the area had rebounded since his first trip to the region.<ref name="wcs" /><ref name="china">{{Cite web|url=http://www.china-embassy.org/eng/zt/mgryzdzg/t36537.htm|title= American Biologist Praises Tibetan Wildlife Conservation|access-date=October 19, 2007|publisher=Chinese Embassy|year=2003|author=Chinese Embassy}}</ref><ref name="npr">{{Cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=7316356|title=A Resurgence of Wildlife in Northern Tibet|access-date=October 19, 2007|publisher=[[National Public Radio]]|year=2007|author=Alex Chadwick}}</ref> Most significantly, the wild [[yak]] population, which was estimated at only 13 individuals, had grown to over 187.<ref name="china" /> "The Tibet Forestry Department has obviously made a dedicated and successful effort in protecting the wildlife." Schaller wrote in a letter to the [[World Wide Fund for Nature|World Wildlife Fund]]'s Dawa Cering.<ref name="china" /> While in Tibet, Schaller worked on researching the rare Tibetan [[antelope]], or chiru, whose population declined due to [[trophy hunting]] for their exotic wool.<ref name="lcaof">{{Cite web|url=http://www.lcaof.org/new.html|title=Current Reports: Observations from a Recent Field Report|access-date=October 20, 2007|publisher=Liz Claiborne and Art Ortenberg Foundation|author1=George B. Schaller|author2=Kang Aili|author3=Cai Xinbin|author4=Liu Yanlin|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071126011804/http://www.lcaof.org/new.html|archive-date=November 26, 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref> Working with Tibetan authorities, and the Liz Claiborne and Art Ortenberg Foundation, Schaller helped protect the breeding and calving grounds of the chiru in the [[Kunlun Mountains|Kunlun mountains]] of [[Xinjiang]] Province.<ref name="lcaof" />

In 2007, Schaller worked with [[Pakistan]], [[Afghanistan]], [[Tajikistan]], and China to develop a new "Peace Park", that would protect {{convert|20000|mi|km}} of habitat for the largest wild sheep species, the [[Marco Polo sheep]].<ref name="lang" /><ref name="hindutwo" /><ref name="Natgeo" /> In danger due to their impressive spiral horns, which can measure up to {{convert|6|ft|m}} in length, the sheep is sought out as a trophy by international hunters.<ref name="lang" /> Schaller's research in the [[Pamir Mountains]] will play an important role in the park's creation.<ref name="lang" /><ref name="time" /><ref name="hindutwo" />

==Conservation results==

Schaller's work in conservation has resulted in the protection of large stretches of area in the [[Amazon rainforest|Amazon]], [[Brazil]], the [[Hindu Kush]] in Pakistan, and forests in Southeast Asia.<ref name="newsci">{{Cite web|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg12617184.500.html|title=On the Trail of the Snow Leopard|access-date=October 19, 2007|work=[[New Scientist]] |year=1990|author=Christopher Joyce}}</ref> Due in part to Schaller's work, over 20 parks or preserves worldwide have been established, including [[Alaska]]'s [[Arctic National Wildlife Refuge]] (ANWR), the Shey-Phoksundo National Park in Nepal, and the [[Changtang Nature Reserve]], one of the world's most significant wildlife refuges.<ref name="lang" /><ref name="man" /><ref name="interview" /><ref name="wcs">{{Cite web|url=http://www.wcs.org/353624/192525|title=WCS Biologist George Schaller Reports Surprising Increase of Wildlife in Tibet|access-date=October 19, 2007|publisher=Wildlife Conservation Society|year=2007|author=Wildlife Conservation Society |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070811015711/http://wcs.org/353624/192525 |archive-date = August 11, 2007}}</ref> At over {{convert|200000|mi|km}},<ref name="npr" /> the Chang Tang Nature Reserve is triple the size of America's largest wildlife refuge, and was called "One of the most ambitious attempts to arrest the shrinkage of natural ecosystems", by ''[[The New York Times]]''.<ref name="cas">{{Cite web|url=http://www.calacademy.org/geninfo/newsroom/releases/2000/schaller0100.html|title=A Conversation with Dr. George Schaller|access-date=October 5, 2007|publisher=[[California Academy of Sciences]]|year=2000|author=California Academy of Sciences|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050912105719/http://www.calacademy.org/geninfo/newsroom/releases/2000/schaller0100.html|archive-date=September 12, 2005|author-link=California Academy of Sciences}}</ref>

==Bigfoot research==
Schaller is one of a few prominent scientists who argue that [[Bigfoot]] reports are worthy of serious study. A 2003 ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' story described Schaller as a "Bigfoot [[skeptic]]", but he also expressed disapproval for other scientists who do not examine evidence, yet "write [Bigfoot] off as a [[hoax]] or [[mythology|myth]]. I don't think that's fair."<ref name="latimes">{{cite news | last =Bailey | first =Eric | title =Bigfoot's Big Feat: New Life; A prankster's deeds revealed posthumously appeared to doom the legend. | pages =section A.1 | work =[[Los Angeles Times]] | date =April 19, 2003 | url =https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/latimes/access/325851481.html?dids=325851481:325851481&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Apr+19%2C+2003&author=Eric+Bailey&pub=Los+Angeles+Times&edition=&startpage=A.1&desc=The+State%3B+COLUMN+ONE%3B+Bigfoot%27s+Big+Feat%3A+New+Life%3B+A+prankster%27s+deeds+revealed+posthumously+appeared+to+doom+the+legend.+But+Sasquatch+still+looms+large%2C+and+scientists+are+intrigued. | access-date =October 5, 2007 | archive-date =March 2, 2013 | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20130302000159/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/latimes/access/325851481.html?dids=325851481:325851481&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Apr+19%2C+2003&author=Eric+Bailey&pub=Los+Angeles+Times&edition=&startpage=A.1&desc=The+State%3B+COLUMN+ONE%3B+Bigfoot%27s+Big+Feat%3A+New+Life%3B+A+prankster%27s+deeds+revealed+posthumously+appeared+to+doom+the+legend.+But+Sasquatch+still+looms+large%2C+and+scientists+are+intrigued. | url-status =dead }}</ref><ref name="bfro2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_article.asp?id=332|title=Bigfoot's Big Feat: New Life|access-date=October 5, 2007|work=Los Angeles Times|year=2003|author=Eric Bailey|via=Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization|archive-date=February 1, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160201153735/http://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_article.asp?id=332|url-status=dead}}</ref> In a 2003 ''[[The Denver Post|Denver Post]]'' article Schaller said that he is troubled that no Bigfoot remains have ever been uncovered, and no feces samples have been found to allow DNA testing. Schaller notes: "There have been so many sightings over the years, even if you throw out 95 percent of them, there ought to be some explanation for the rest. I think a hard-eyed look is absolutely essential".<ref name="post">{{Cite news|url=http://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_article.asp?id=328|title=Bigfoot Believers: Legitimate scientific study of legend gains backing of top primate experts|access-date=October 5, 2007|page=1|via=Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization|work=[[The Denver Post]]|date=January 5, 2003|author=Theo Stein|archive-date=February 1, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160201153735/http://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_article.asp?id=328|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="post2">{{Cite news|url=http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=DP&p_theme=dp&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&p_topdoc=1&p_text_direct-0=0F86B5F3CA2AE03C&p_field_direct-0=document_id&p_perpage=10&p_sort=YMD_date:D&s_trackval=GooglePM|title=Bigfoot Believers: Legitimate scientific study of legend gains backing of top primate experts|access-date=October 5, 2007|work=The Denver Post|year=2003|author=Theo Stein|via=[[NewsBank]]}}</ref>

== Publications ==

Schaller has written more than fifteen books on African and Asian [[mammal]]s, including ''Serengeti Lion: A Study of [[Predator]]–[[Prey]] Relations'', ''The Last Panda'', and ''Tibet's Hidden Wilderness'', ''Tibet the Wild'', based on his own studies, and supported by long-term observations of species in their natural [[Habitat (ecology)|habitat]]s. Schaller has also written hundreds of magazine articles, and dozens of books and scientific articles about [[tiger]]s, [[jaguar]]s, [[cheetah]]s and [[leopard]]s, as well as wild sheep and goats, [[rhinoceroses]], and [[flamingo]]s. Over more than five decades, Schaller's field research has helped shape wildlife protection efforts around the world.<ref name="lang" /><ref name="man" /><ref name="cas" /><ref name="Natgeo" />

==Awards and recognition==

Schaller's conservation honors include National Geographic's Lifetime Achievement Award,<ref name="lang" /> 
a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]],<ref name="uofaf">{{Cite web|url=https://news.uaf.edu/news/a_news/20060712093558.html|title=Noted wildlife expert returns to Alaska|access-date=October 20, 2007|publisher=[[University of Alaska]]|year=2006|author=Doreen Fitzgerald|archive-date=June 4, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210604070454/https://news.uaf.edu/news/a_news/20060712093558.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the [[World Wildlife Fund]]'s Gold Medal for: "''Contributions to the understanding and conservation of [[endangered species]]''".<ref name="msu" /> 
Schaller has also been awarded the [[International Cosmos Prize]],<ref name="icp" />
the [[Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement]],<ref name="tyler">
{{Cite web| url=http://www.usc.edu/dept/LAS/tylerprize/tyler1997.html|title=Tyler Prize Laureates|access-date=October 20, 2007|publisher=[[University of Southern California]] College of Letters, Arts & Sciences|year=1997|author=Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070808034758/http://www.usc.edu/dept/LAS/tylerprize/tyler1997.html <!--Added by H3llBot-->|archive-date=August 8, 2007}}</ref> 
and he was the first recipient of the Wildlife Conservation Society's Beebe Fellowship.<ref name="uofaf" /> 
Schaller's literary honors include the U.S. [[National Book Award]] [[List of winners of the National Book Award#Science, Philosophy and Religion|in Science]] (for ''The Serengeti Lion'' in 1973).<ref name=nba1973>
[https://www.nationalbook.org/people/george-b-schaller/ "National Book Awards – 1973"]. [[National Book Foundation]]. Retrieved March 7, 2012.</ref> In 1988, Schaller received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url= https://www.achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration/}}</ref> 
In September 2008, he received the [[Indianapolis Prize]] for his work in animal conservation.<ref name="indy">
{{Cite web|url=http://www.indianapolisprize.org/content.aspx?CID=798|title=Distinguished Field Biologist George B. Schaller Named Winner of the 2008 Indianapolis Prize|access-date=September 29, 2008|publisher=Indianapolis Zoological Society|year=2008|author=Indianapolis Zoological Society|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080910203604/http://www.indianapolisprize.org/content.aspx?cid=798 <!--Added by H3llBot-->|archive-date=September 10, 2008}}</ref>

In 2017, a newly discovered species of scorpion was named as ''Liocheles schalleri'' in his honor.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Mirza|first=Zeeshan A.|date=December 17, 2017|title=Description of a new species of Liocheles Sundevall, 1833 (Hormuridae) from India|url=https://biotaxa.org/Zootaxa/article/view/zootaxa.4365.2.6|journal=Zootaxa|volume=4365|issue=2|pages=217–230|doi=10.11646/zootaxa.4365.2.6|pmid=29686218|issn=1175-5334|url-access=subscription}}
*{{cite news |date=December 20, 2017 |title=Tiny scorpion packs a punch |newspaper=The Hindu |url=https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/energy-and-environment/tiny-scorpion-packs-a-punch/article22084724.ece}}</ref>

== Personal life ==

His wife Kay majored in Anthropology at the University of Alaska in Fairbanks, where she and Schaller met. They married in 1957 and Kay assisted in fieldwork and edited and typed his manuscripts for nearly seven decades.
Kay Schaller died on March 7, 2023 at the age of 93.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/litchfieldcountytimes/name/kay-schaller-obituary?id=50997014 | title=Kay Schaller Obituary (2023) - Lebanon, NH - Litchfield County Times | website=[[Legacy.com]] }}</ref>

The couple had two sons.
